about.title: From the first call to production.
about.p1: Every project starts with a 30-minute call: you explain the problem, we explain how we would build it. If it fits, we send a fixed-scope proposal, then a clickable prototype before a single line of production code.
about.p2: During the build, you see working software early and often, and we measure the result by real usage rather than by the demo. At Monka, the caregiver app, the nurses' CRM and the clinical engine went live in two months, and a new version has shipped roughly every two days since. At LocService, the assistant's drafts are used on 87% of tickets.
about.p3: Then there are two options: we hand the code over to your team with the documentation and runbooks, or we keep running it. With Theodo, training the teams is part of the job, so they adopt these practices themselves and move faster.

about.kicker: // WHY WE BUILD OUR OWN PRODUCTS
about.title: Our first client is us.
about.p1: The Vibe Company is an AI agency, and a good part of what we know how to do, we first built for ourselves. Each of these products starts from a friction we lived with every day: sharing the report an agent just produced, organizing the team's skills, giving our agents a memory, coordinating several coding agents on one project, or simply not losing an idea thrown out in a meeting.
about.p2: Several of them run the agency every day: Bruno for the company to-do, Skillpack for our skills, Granite for our agents' memory. That is how we learn what holds up in production and what breaks, before we bring it to a client. If our own company does not run better with our tools, we have no legitimacy selling them.
about.p3: Most of them are open source and published on GitHub, often under the MIT license: you can read the code, run them yourself or borrow ideas from them. Quivr, the open-source engine the company grew out of, is on the list too. Each page explains why we built the product, how it works and who it is for.

problem.title: Classic security tools are no longer enough on their own
problem.p1: The surface to protect has changed: dozens of SaaS tools wired into your data, coding agents opening pull requests, years of accumulated configs and permissions. Each tool sees its own slice; nobody sees the whole.
problem.p2: A one-off audit or a quarterly scan captures a state that drifts the very next day: a role widened “temporarily”, a dependency bumped, a bucket opened for a test. CTOs, CISOs and platform leads need a continuous loop, not one more report.
problem.p3: Recent incidents are a reminder: exposed secrets and legacy runtimes are still open doors. We broke them down in <link>Black October: what it means for AI agents</link>.

whatFor.q: What does Quivr do for me, in plain words?
whatFor.a: It keeps every article, email and post, even when a service goes down, and keeps the earlier version when one is corrected. It lets you search by meaning, not just keywords, and shows the exact passage. And it tells your app when a new article matches a topic you described, with the reason it matched.

underTheHood.a: A Go engine, one binary for the API, the worker and migrations, on PostgreSQL, S3-compatible storage and Temporal. Search runs on Weaviate, by keyword and by vector, with multilingual E5 embeddings. It exposes an HTTP API (v0), signed webhooks, a change feed (polling or SSE) and MCP for AI agents.

v1.a: Quivr V2 replaced the V1 code base on the main branch. V1 is preserved at the v1-final tag, the last commit of Quivr V1, so you can still read, fork or run it from there.

license.a: MIT. It is free to use, modify and self-host. Some plugins rely on libraries with their own license, such as pypdf (BSD-3-Clause) for the PDF plugin.

production.q: Can I use Quivr V2 in production?
production.a: Not yet. Quivr V2 is at the evaluation stage and its API is v0, which may change without notice. Try it on your machine with the Quickstart, and talk to us if you want to plan a production rollout.

selfHost.a: Yes. Quivr runs on servers you control, next to your application: one machine with Docker Compose to evaluate it, or a deployment with separate workers and a dedicated vector host. By default, Quivr itself sends document text nowhere outside your installation.

support.a: For questions and bugs, use the issues and discussions of the GitHub repository. For business plugins, planning a production rollout, or hosting that works to HDS requirements for health data, The Vibe Company can help as a service: book a call.

hds.title: HDS: who is certified, and where we work
hds.intro: The question is often framed the wrong way. Here is the split, as we practise it.

host.label: HDS host
host.desc: Cloud or managed-service provider, certified for the activities of the framework it performs.

us.label: The Vibe Company
us.desc: Development partner: we build inside, without taking the data out.

host.title: The certification is the host's
host.desc: HDS certification covers the host and the activities of the French Digital Health Agency's framework that it performs. It does not automatically extend to the software publisher, or to the agency that builds the product.

environment.title: We build inside your environment
environment.desc: Your HDS host is often already chosen. We develop inside it, with the access you grant us, and the code, logs and test environments stay there.

ai.title: AI pitfalls, handled at design time
ai.desc: Model calls, logs, test environments, transfers outside the EEA: that is where an AI project leaves the perimeter without noticing. We settle them before the first line of code.

gdpr.title: HDS does not replace GDPR
gdpr.desc: HDS covers hosting. GDPR covers the whole processing: purpose, minimisation, retention, data subject rights.

proof.title: What we shipped at Monka
proof.intro: Monka supports people who care for a loved one, with coordinating nurses and partner insurers. We took over their existing API and CRM, and built inside their HDS environment.
points: A caregiver app: a 165-question assessment that leads to an action plan, the circle of close ones, a chat with the nurse, and appointment booking.
Lifeline, the CRM for coordinating nurses.
A versioned clinical engine: 12 versions of the framework, without breaking the app.
A partner API with signed webhooks, so insurers can follow the people they cover.
In production in two months, then 90 app releases in six months: one roughly every two days.
Encrypted, GDPR-compliant health data, inside the HDS environment Monka already had. We never stepped outside it.
proof.other: LocService: an agent drafts the reply to every ticket, connected to internal APIs; a human reviews and decides. Drafts used on 87% of tickets.

certified.a: No. We are not a health data host. We build to GDPR and HDS requirements, usually inside the HDS environment the client already has, as in the case shown on this page.

needCertification.q: Do you need HDS certification to launch a healthcare AI product?
needCertification.a: Often it is the host (and sometimes the software publisher, depending on who has access) that falls within the scope. We clarify the split of activities during scoping. The details are in our HDS article.

timeline.a: It depends on the foundation. A real example: at a healthcare client whose HDS environment was already in place, the app, the CRM and the clinical engine went live in two months. We do not quote a generic timeline.

llm.q: Do you send patient records to LLMs?
llm.a: We design so that health data never leaves the agreed framework: a model inside the perimeter, pseudonymisation before the call, or no external call at all. No magic promises.

cost.q: How much does a project cost?
cost.a: We set the scope after the call and the scoping, in a written proposal. There is no public rate card.

service.name: AI agent deployment to production
service.description: Deploying business AI agents inside a company, from POC to the daily run: scoping the first workflow, skills connected to existing tools, authority and guardrails, memory and context, observability, run and handoff. Sensitive actions stay approved by a human.

problem.title: A POC doesn't die for lack of a model — it dies for lack of production
problem.p1: The demo works. Then the real questions arrive: which permissions the agent gets, on which tools (whose APIs change or go down), who owns it when it gets things wrong, and which metric says it is useful. With no answers, nobody dares let it act, and the pilot stays a pilot.
problem.p2: COOs, heads of support and product CTOs are not waiting for one more slide. They want a first agent that is useful in real conditions, wired into their systems, that their teams use every day.
problem.p3: New to the topic? Start with our <link>guide to AI agents for business</link>. This page is about deploying one with you.

offer.title: What an agent deployment at your company includes
offer.intro: Six building blocks, delivered in your environment and on your tools. Not one more chat silo: an agent that works where your teams already work.

scope.title: Scoping the first workflow
scope.desc: We find where the time really goes, with a simple grid: volume × repetitiveness × risk. We pick one workflow, not ten.

skills.title: Skills and tools
skills.desc: Versioned skills and connections to the systems you already run: CRM, support tool, knowledge base, internal APIs.

authority.title: Authority and guardrails
authority.desc: What the agent may read, propose and do, written down in black and white. Sensitive actions go through human approval.

memory.title: Memory and context
memory.desc: Tickets, documentation, customer history: the agent works from your real context, within the scope agreed together, and no further.

observability.title: Observability
observability.desc: Logs of every action, acceptance rate of its proposals, escalations to a human: you see what the agent does and what it is worth.

run.title: Run and handoff
run.desc: Runbooks, training for your teams, or joint operation: the agent has an owner the day it goes to production.

offer.complement: Complementary to our <hardening>AI agents to harden your product and stack</hardening> (the security of your infrastructure) and to our article on <authority>agent authority</authority> (in French; what an agent is allowed to do).

proof.intro: Case studies published on this site, with their numbers. Nothing else.

cases.locservice: An agent drafts the reply to every ticket, connected to internal APIs, on hundreds of tickets a day. A human reviews and decides: the drafts are used on 87% of tickets.
cases.coup-de-pates: Quality-control AI skills that check product documents (labels, specifications) and flag every discrepancy, alongside Ensemble, the employee CSR app.

chatbot.title: Not a generic chatbot
chatbot.desc: A chat with no tools and no context does not change how your teams work. Here, the agent is wired into your systems and has a precise role.

replace.title: Not “we replace your support team”
replace.desc: The agent takes the repetitive part. Your teams keep the decisions, the customer relationship and the hard cases.

hardening.title: Not our hardening offer
hardening.desc: Hardening secrets, IAM or CI with a fleet of agents is a different page.
hardening.link: AI agents to harden your product and stack

promise.title: Not a compliance or zero-error promise
promise.desc: An agent sometimes gets things wrong. We design it so the error shows, reaches a human and gets fixed, and we document what was done.

start.q: Which process should we start with?
start.a: A high-volume process, with fairly stable rules, where an agent's mistake stays contained. Often the agent starts by writing a draft rather than sending directly.

timeline.q: How long until an agent is useful?
timeline.a: We work in short cycles, and we won't give you a generic timeline before we have seen the process. On our published customer support case, the agent's drafts are used on 87% of tickets, out of several hundred tickets a day.

existing.q: What if we already have an in-house POC?
existing.a: We start from what exists: tools, prompts, and the authority debt that has piled up (what the agent can do without anyone having decided it). We industrialize rather than rewrite everything.

data.a: We work to GDPR and HDS requirements. When health data is involved, the agent runs inside the client's covered environment. We claim no certification we do not hold.
